2027 NBA Draft Substantial Board: Quentin Coleman's meteoric rise, Tyran Stokes stays at No. 1, returners boost stock

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1689 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the first thing to know about the 2027 draft cycle is that it remains wide open.
  • But after three full weeks of college basketball and heading into a Thanksgiving week full of high-profile matchups, we have updated the 2027 NBA Draft Big Board.
  • Inside the front offices of the 30 NBA organizations, most have yet to even start ranking prospects.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the first thing to know about the 2027 draft cycle is that it remains wide open. There are still eight months to go before Adam Silver steps up to the podium to announce the first pick. Nothing has been decided yet. In fact, there's probably only about ten players total that can confidently say they expect to be a first-round pick at this point. Everything else is yet to be determined.

But after three full weeks of college basketball and heading into a Thanksgiving week full of high-profile matchups, we have updated the 2027 NBA Draft Big Board.

Inside the front offices of the 30 NBA organizations, most have yet to even start ranking prospects. They're still building their lists, sorting them into tiers, and will spend the coming months trying to establish their order.

According to recent reports, that's the biggest difference between those front offices and the public discourse about the draft. The fans want answers now, and the Twitter scouts are quick to make bold statements in hopes of saying they were right first. The experts who actually do this for a living recognize that the sole goal is to be right on draft night, and doing that requires them to not jump to any early conclusions.

That's all critical context to understanding this big board update, which is, at best, a way too early look at the most relevant prospects. It should be interpreted in tiers. There are probably five or six prospects competing for the top of the draft, but that list could change. Maybe 11 who should feel good about their chances to be first-round picks. Everything beyond that is simply a battle that will continue to play out over the course of the next 8 months. Let's dive into the biggest storylines after three weeks of college basketball action.

I got a first-hand look at Stokes last week at the Player's Era 8 in Las Vegas. He went down with a contusion midway through his first game, sat out the second, and returned to drop 22 points and 11 rebounds in the final. In totality, the signs of extreme growth that have characterized his early season play continued to be evident in Vegas. He was far and away the most talented player in high school basketball a year ago, but had developed a history of not living up to his potential, or at least not impacting winning to the degree that someone with his talent should. So, coming into his year at Kansas, the eyeballs were more about his maturity, reliability, and approach. Answering those questions has gone about as well as it possibly could so far. He's not only been engaged and impactful, but he's shown connectivity with Bill Self that makes him look coachable. He's also not gotten easily derailed by adversity, which is a reassuring data point.

Industry observers note that to be clear, for as good as he's been, there's still plenty of room for improvement. In high school, he had an instinctive way of improvising his way to the rim. In college, he's found that isn't quite as easy, even with someone like Tre Kaufman-Renn regularly clearing the way for him anytime he comes charging at the rim. So, while he's over-dribbling at times, his playmaking is real, he's asserted himself as a rebounder, his shooting is progressing, and he's starting to use his size in the post.

It has been revealed that the bottom line is this: most teams are looking for a potential alpha-type creator with the first pick. Stokes is your best bet in the 2027 cycle, by a relatively large margin at this point, but it's still too early to say he's a lock to go number one. I'd put that at about 70% at this point. Getting to the finish line will require him to continue trending in the right direction, making sure teams are comfortable with their due diligence in the pre-draft process, and also leaving open the possibility for someone else to emerge in the coming months.

Speaking of ascending prospects, no one has moved the needle more in the first three weeks of the season than Illinois' freshman Quentin Coleman. But for those who track draft prospects 365 days a year, the last three weeks are just a short spurt in what has been a rapid rise over the course of the last 15 months.

In the 2025 EYBL season, Coleman averaged 11.8 points. 5.1 rebounds and 2.4 assists for a Brad Beal Elite team that won the Peach Jam Championship. To put it plainly, he was a role player, albeit a valuable one, on a team that was built around current Arkansas freshman JJ Andrews and utilized Trey Pearson, who is currently a freshman at High Point, as their primary ball-handler and distributor.

Recent findings suggest that as soon as Coleman's high school season began, though, we immediately saw signs of growth. Those signs continued throughout the course of the year, and he skyrocketed the rankings in the process. He also decommitted from Wake Forest and took a much bigger NIL payday from Illinois. While he finished with five-star status, it was immediately clear at the USA Basketball trials in May that even that was too low.

It has been revealed that since arriving at Illinois, Coleman has continued the pattern of exceeding expectations. His skill level, feel for the game, defensive instincts, and nose for the ball are all as impressive as expected. The physical transition has been easier than expected. He's continued to develop more burst, physicality, and, as a result, playmaking.

At the moment, he's moved all the way up to No. 4 on the CBS's current 2027 NBA Draft Massive Board, but we're not going to put a cap on what he could do given the unprecedented growth we've witnessed over the last 15 months.

In a recent development, there were a number of prospects who had a chance to be first-round picks in last year's draft, who opted to return to college basketball. While most, if not all, of them are probably making more money in college this year than they would have in the NBA, they are also making strides with their game, and in the process, helping their draft stock in what is widely viewed as a weaker draft than last year's.

We've been bullish on Amari Allen's chances of helping himself given his fresh on-ball role at Alabama, and so far, he's done just that. The 16 points, 6 assists, and 5 rebounds per game on 52/50/82 shooting showcases both the versatility and shooting gains we were banking on. Most of all, though, it's his decision-making with the ball that has been glaring. His usage has gone way up, and his turnovers have gone way down. He has recorded 30 assists against just three turnovers through the first five games of the season. Add his hyper-competitiveness to the equation, and he's certainly helping himself.

Arizona massive man Motiejus Krivas looked like an NBA-ready defender last year. This year, it's been more of the same. He's massive, even by NBA standards, at 7-foot-2 and 260 pounds, but deceptively versatile and very smart with his angles. We're also seeing definite growth offensively, particularly with his skill set facing the basket. Last week's 18-point, 12-rebound, 4-block performance against UConn was one that captured all of his value, and a game that scouts will undoubtedly revisit.

Meanwhile, his teammate, Ivan Kharchenkov, has gone from a defensive role player to Arizona's featured scorer, and is putting up nearly 23 points, 8 rebounds, and 5 assists per game. To put it plainly, he's been as good of a two-way player as there is in the country, and now looks like he could be trending towards the draft lottery.

Florida's Thomas Haugh had a chance to be a mid-first-round pick last June, but the variable that gave many scouts pause was his shooting. This year, he's shooting it with much more confidence and rhythm, making 18 of his 34 attempts through his first five games. Simultaneously, he's continuing to do all the little things that made him so intriguing in the first place with his motor, physicality, rebounding, and defensive versatility.

Speaking of shooting, Braylon Mullins is establishing himself as one of the nation's premier shooters, as expected, despite the fact that he's clearly not 100% healthy. Through his first five games, he's made 19 threes on 50 attempts, but it's been the types of shots that have really stood out. He's running all over the court, flying off screens, and making threes on the move, all while being the focal point of opposing defenses. In short, Mullins is making the type of tough shots that translate to the next level, despite not having his typical ability to separate.

One of the defining characteristics of the national 2026 recruiting class was the number of prospects who had glaring potential, but had yet to put it all together. That list included the likes of Duke's Cameron Williams,  Ohio State's Anthony Thompson, Maryland's Baba Oladotun, Christian Collins,  Adonis Rayliff and Darius Ratliff, all at USC. Nevertheless, almost all of them commanded the type of recruitment and correlating financial commitment that suggested programs were willing to invest in their development.

So far In t those investments have not resulted in the types of gains we had hoped for. The Ratliffs, Adonis in particular, have revealed some flashes, while Collins has only recently been cleared. Williams and Oladotun are barely in the rotation, and Thompson is playing, but not making the type of impact that anyone hoped.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we're now a month into the 2026-27 NBA season, and while we're still weeks away from the unofficial start of trade season (Dec. 15), we've seen enough basketball for teams to at least begin making plans for the upcoming transaction cycle. Teams are starting to know how good they are, what sort of holes they're dealing with and what the market is going to look like as we draw closer to the February trade deadline.

Firm rumors are still in short supply, but we're at least getting some early buzz on who plans to do what in the months to come. So let's check in on what has made the rounds lately.

The 14-3 Los Angeles Lakers are headed for a titanic clash with the San Antonio Spurs on Friday that will presumably put one of those two teams in pole position in the Western Conference. Last Friday, however, head of basketball operations Rob Pelinka did a pregame interview with Spectrum SportsNet in which he made it clear he looks to be aggressive ahead of February's deadline.

Sources indicate that "We'll be active at the trade deadline to shore up things that we see," Pelinka said. "We think this team has a real chance to make a run, so we want to give the group as much talent as we can. Don't want to get too far over our skis with a hot start, because you don't want to get massive-headed, but clearly the way it's gone so far, it's been great and we hope it continues.".

The Lakers are very limited in terms of tradable draft capital because of their significant July swing for Walker Kessler. They only have one first-round asset available, and it's only swap rights in 2032. They picked up two useful second-round picks in the Deandre Ayton trade, though, giving them three in total. That's not enough for a blockbuster, but it's helpful liquidity. Further, the Lakers are relatively financially flexible going into the deadline as well. They're barely over the luxury-tax line and have around $8 million in room beneath their first apron hard cap, allowing them to potentially make a somewhat unbalanced trade if the need presents itself.

It has been revealed that so, what would the Lakers be looking for at the deadline? Two obvious needs stand out:.

In a recent development, as Marc Stein noted, the Los Angeles Clippers have moved to a veteran-only starting lineup, with Darius Garland, Rui Hachimura, Derrick Jones Jr., Max Strus and Brook Lopez opening games lately. Brandon Ingram, returning Monday, is sure to join that group, and Kris Dunn is a central part of their rotation. All of these players but Ingram and Garland are on expiring deals, and Stein noted that the Clippers are "regarded as a certain seller" ahead of the trade deadline.

And, well, that makes plenty of sense. The Clippers were just stripped of five first-round picks in the Kawhi Leonard scandal. Those expiring contracts belong to players who almost certainly won't be a part of the next great Clipper team, but they could help replenish the team's draft capital moving forward.

The Clippers are, by far, the most versatile seller on the market right now. In theory, they could burnish just about any contender. Need defense? Jones and Dunn have you covered. Offense? Strus and Hachimura are proven playoff snipers. The center market is in the middle of a supply-demand crisis. Lopez has been sensational this season and could give any contender a solid 20 minutes per night. With Keaton Wagler in the building, it's hard to imagine they'd even shut the door on a good enough Garland offer. Expect the Clippers to live in the rumor mill for the next few months. They have several players who could legitimately impact the championship hunt.

According to recent reports, last week, SNY dropped a stunner of a rumor: that the Utah Jazz, loaded with young guards and off to a terrible start, had had internal conversations about pursuing Mavericks guard Kyrie Irving. The rumor didn't make much sense in the moment, and The Salt Lake Tribune reported Monday that the Jazz "don't appear to have any real interest" in the future Hall of Famer.

They have, however, talked trade with the team we just discussed: the Clippers. Those conversations began with "various Clippers bigs" and have moved on to wing depth, of which the Clippers have plenty. The Jazz are reportedly casting a wide net in pursuit of help.

Recent findings suggest that the 3-15 Jazz have been among the NBA's biggest disappointments this season. A lot of that has been the result of injuries, with Jaren Jackson Jr. and Lauri Markkanen out now and Jusuf Nurkić having not yet debuted this season. The Jazz are painfully thin in the front court at this point, and the early partnership between Keyonte George and Darryn Peterson in the backcourt has yielded mixed results.

Casting a wide net makes sense since the Jazz could theoretically use help basically anywhere. More of a playmaking guard to balance out the score-first instincts that George and Peterson bring would make sense. Wing depth, especially defense-first wing depth, would help address a major weakness. Dunn is a former Jazz player. And of course, adding some size to deal with all of those injuries would probably have the biggest immediate impact. Utah doesn't control its own first-round pick this year. The Jazz benefit from losing in no way, and that has seemingly made them eager to try to fight an uphill battle back into the Western Conference Play-In race.

#153352. Man for Man: How Brighton’s Press Suffocated Arsenal

Man for Man: How Brighton’s Press Suffocated Arsenal

📅 23 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3214 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Spielverlagerung

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • von Next Generation am 23.09.2026 in den Kategorien Premier League,Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren.
  • Recent findings suggest that brBrighton arrived at the match fresh off a 3–2 win at Old Trafford, while Arsenal boasted a clean defensive record and a reputation for controlling games and seeing them out like few other teams in Europe.
  • Recent findings suggest that arteta’s Arsenal are among the best sides in Europe at controlling games out of possession.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

von Next Generation am 23.09.2026 in den Kategorien Premier League,Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren.

Recent findings suggest that brBrighton arrived at the match fresh off a 3–2 win at Old Trafford, while Arsenal boasted a clean defensive record and a reputation for controlling games and seeing them out like few other teams in Europe. The match ended 3–0, sparking immense hype around Brighton’s pressing. This analysis explores the underlying mechanisms: their man-oriented pressing across the entire pitch, their asymmetrical build-up play, their transition behavior after winning the ball, and the three goals themselves.

Recent findings suggest that arteta’s Arsenal are among the best sides in Europe at controlling games out of possession. Any opponent who sets out to establish order is playing on the ground Arsenal own. Hürzeler therefore decided against control – not control surrendered in the sense of a low block, but a chaotic game state that Brighton generated themselves and were therefore prepared for.

System & movement with the ball – FC Arsenal.

System & movement with the ball – Brighton & Hove Albion.

According to recent reports, the thread running through ninety minutes: Arsenal were not to settle into an organised phase either with or without the ball. Three decisions delivered that. The build-up was set up asymmetrically – on the right Brighton prepared the long ball and occupied the landing zone before it was played, on the left counter-movements opened the short route. It was never long instead of short, but two prepared options that would have demanded opposite answers from Arsenal. After regains the ball was not secured but risked immediately, because a secured ball gives the opponent exactly the seconds they need to reorganise. And the press lived off intensity and constantly fresh starting points: when a line was played through, Brighton did not stand still but re-established their shape and triggered again.

All three decisions give up ball control in the classical sense. Control came instead from preparation – if you know where the ball will land and you are standing there beforehand, you control the situation without the ball.

Recent findings suggest that what followed can be pinned to a single number: 41 Arsenal turnovers in their own danger zone. That is not a figure a side of this quality produces because they play badly, but because they never reached the game state their build-up is designed for.

Brightons manorientated press against a 4-3-3.

The press was simple in principle and demanding in execution. Brighton set up with man-reference to their direct opponent and switched into pure man-marking on the trigger. Against a side that tracks from the first second, marking assignments can be pulled apart by movement before any pressure exists; Brighton refused to offer that, because their shape stayed compact until the trigger moment.

In the “mid-block,” positioned +1 on the last line, but ready at any moment to transition into a high press upon a pressing trigger.

Recent findings suggest that the steering began with Ayari. He curved his pressing run so that Konsa stayed in his cover shadow and Raya was forced to the other side. Kostoulas marked Gabriel, while Chema Andrés and Groß pushed aggressively onto Arsenal’s No. 8s. Groß in particular tracked the dropping Rice and at times advanced into the first pressing line, in some sequences all the way onto Konsa. That requires Rice to be picked up by a team-mate in the same moment – the man-marking worked through handovers as much as through tracking. Centrally, the striker and the No. 10 rotated accordingly: whoever had the shorter route to the next man on the ball pushed out, while the other covered behind him and took over again on the next trigger.

Recent findings suggest that it only held up because the centre-backs came with it. Vušković and Struijk stepped out onto Ødegaard and the dropping Havertz and prevented an underload in central areas. When Arsenal built with three in the first line, Brighton kept one centre-back zonal in the back line – but with permanent reference to the unmarked player in the No. 6 space, stepping onto him the moment the press was triggered. Arsenal’s numerical advantage in build-up therefore never translated into a free man anywhere on the pitch.

Industry observers note that raya was part of the marking scheme too. Ayari’s cover shadow left only the route through a No. 6, and under man-marking that is not an escape but a duel that begins with the first touch. Raya’s body shape reinforced it: he tended to open only half-way, which effectively removed the switch to the far side from his repertoire. Steered onto his right foot, only the right-hand build-up side remained; the left lay open for long stretches and was unreachable for the one player who could have found it.

Every back pass served as a trigger. When the ball went back to Raya or the centre-backs, Brighton pushed up as a unit and raised the defensive line. The density around the ball came less from the base shape than from the recovery runs: players who had been beaten sprinted back, and they did not run at the ball but with a cover shadow onto the lay-off option behind it. An Arsenal player with a marker in his back therefore had neither the lay-off nor the chance to turn.

According to recent reports, this is precisely where Brighton differed from most sides who get played through against Arsenal. The usual response is to stay deep once a line has been broken and wait for the shape to settle. Brighton instead pushed up into the next line and used the mid-block to prepare the next jump back into the high press – even when that press had just been beaten. The press therefore had not one starting point per possession, but a steady supply of upcoming ones, and Arsenal had to solve the same pressure several times within a single attack.

It has been revealed that arsenal’s core problem was the absence of a threat in behind. Their attempts to play through the press came without pace beyond the back line, so Brighton were never forced to turn towards their own goal. That made the press cheap: no threat in behind, therefore no need to drop the line. There are three answers to committed man-marking – movement that drags your own marker away and opens space for a third player, a dribble that beats the assignment one-on-one, or a target man who wins the long balls. Arsenal produced none of them.

When the high press was beaten, Brighton dropped into a 5-1-4 and inverted the priority. The five in the last line formed a deliberate overload against Arsenal’s front line – in exactly the moment a man-oriented side is most vulnerable, because its players are facing forward while the opponents are already moving. Brighton took the depth out of the situation first and only then thought about the ball again.

According to recent reports, A “mid-block” in a 5-1-4 formation. The foremost players protected the “red zone” by using their cover shadows and shifting extremely compactly. Arsenal was mostly forced to play around the block, repeatedly giving Brighton time to reorganize.

A single No. 6 held the connection in front, while the four most advanced players stayed narrow and closed the centre with cover shadows rather than pressing the ball carrier. Arsenal found no central switch on the ball-near side and had to play around the block. Every trip around it cost seconds that Brighton used to shift across, so the end of the route offered the same congestion as the start. In some phases six players stood in the last line.

According to recent reports, the block was not a terminus. At every Arsenal back pass Brighton jumped out again and restarted the high press – the same trigger as in the high phase, only from a deeper starting position. The spare man in the last line made that possible, usually Vušković: because the overload left him without a fixed opponent, he could step out, cover the depth and pick up a man himself a moment later. That freed a midfielder to push forward without leaving an assignment open behind him – precisely the point at which sides with a similar approach usually come apart.

In the “mid-block” phase, the “+1” players organized themselves to execute early handovers and jump into pressing situations. Here, Vuskovic—acting as the “+1” player from the defensive line—steps up to pick up the Arsenal player operating in the number 10 position.

Recent findings suggest that on top of that came the trap on the touchline. Once Brighton steered the ball wide, players jumped in from every direction: the ball-near winger closed the route back, the No. 6 covered inside, the back line stepped out. The back pass, the switch and the ball in behind did not disappear one after another but at the same time. Take away only the back pass and a side switches play; take away only the switch and they play backwards and start again. When all that remains is an individual action against several opponents with the touchline at your back, it almost always ends with the opposition.

After a regain there are two basic options: risk the ball immediately to launch the attack, or secure it to establish order. Hürzeler consistently chose the first, and it follows directly from the overall idea – a secured ball would have given Arsenal exactly the seconds in which their structure reorganises.

It has been revealed that when a high press was bypassed, Brighton succeeded in forcing Arsenal into congested situations in the area in front of the back four. In doing so, the players who had been bypassed shifted to block the passing lanes of the players positioned behind the ball. This created additional pressure on the ball carrier, who was simultaneously facing pressure from the front via a “negative” pressing movement (i.e., pressing towards their own goal).

The counter was prepared before the regain. When Arsenal found a player in the No. 6 space after beating the press, Brighton immediately closed his back pass, so the turnover inevitably occurred in a moment when Arsenal were all ahead of the ball. The density around the ball, a defensive necessity, meant in attack that Brighton were central and therefore on the shortest route to goal. The first ball went to the deepest player, followed by a dribble at speed into the box, with no intermediate step and no square pass for safety.

In the build-up phase, Brighton utilized a diamond shape. De Cuyper and Boscagli engaged in a 2v2 duel on the left flank, while Kostoulas, Gomez, and Kadioglu created a high 3v3 situation on the right. Briefly, both center-backs and a defensive midfielder would spread out to widen the formation. Additional support occasionally came from Groß, dropping back from the number 10 position. Ayari occupied Konsa and Gabriel through constant runs into the open spaces ahead of him.

In a recent development, in deep build-up Brighton baited Arsenal in deliberately. Verbruggen put his foot on the ball while the centre-backs split and lengthened the pressing runs of their opponents. On paper that produced a 3v2 against Arsenal’s first line – except Hürzeler had no intention of playing through that overload on the ground. 25 of 40 goalkeeper passes were long, 62.5 per cent, and they went overwhelmingly to the right.

The structure allowed for a long ball to the right flank, feeding into the 3-3 formation. This created opportunities to contest the second ball or flick on the aerial pass. Additionally, Vuskovic offered a short, low passing option as the free player.

Recent findings suggest that there, Brighton consistently created a 3v3 – an intact structure for the second ball regardless of whether the first contact was won. That is exactly what separates it from an ordinary long ball: the action was not judged by the aerial duel but by the situation that followed it. Kostoulas dropping added to the disorganisation of Arsenal’s high line, because a centre-back had to decide whether to follow him between the lines or let him turn. After winning second balls Brighton played on at high speed and looked for an early shot or an early cross, even against a defensive overload – again the decision for tempo over the clean attack.

Once again, the 3-3 structure on the right flank. Here, from open play.

On the left Brighton worked through pinning rather than through length. Boscagli stepping inside dragged Saka into central areas and took him out of the wide zone Arsenal needed him in defensively, while De Cuyper dropped and offered the mid-range diagonal once the assignments had been pulled apart. The asymmetry was a personnel decision: the players for second balls were on the right, the players who could drag markers out of position on the left. Arsenal would have had to condense against one side and hand over assignments cleanly against the other.

The team’s build-up play was asymmetrical, featuring a high, wide approach on the right contrasted with the left flank: Boscagli often played an inverted role—supplementing the existing diamond formation—which opened up space for de Cuyper. Meanwhile, Groß and Kostoulas occupied the players on Arsenal’s right defensive flank, enabling Brighton to find low-ball solutions against the press.

With the ball in midfield there were two patterns. The first was the deliberate back pass to Verbruggen to pull Arsenal’s block out, followed by the same long-short structure as in deep build-up. The back pass was not a safety option here but the tool that created the space behind the pressing line in the first place.

The second pattern worked through central and wide tension at high speed, supplemented by rotations within their own structure. Arsenal repeatedly failed to hand over their pressing assignments in a coordinated way against it – the same weakness Brighton had solved cleanly in their own press. In possession Brighton’s shape approached a 4-3-3: Chema Andrés as the deepest No. 6, Groß with freedom from the left half-space, Kadıoğlu pushing up early to support Gómez, Boscagli starting slightly deeper on the left.

The 1-0 by Groß in the 31st minute is the whole proposal in one sequence. Brighton play back to the goalkeeper from midfield, go long, lose the first contact and win the second ball. After a phase of circulation the next attack meets a back line that has already been destabilised: Kostoulas drops, Arsenal’s midfield and Konsa step out, and Kostoulas lays the ball back against the direction of the pressure to Groß. Because Ayari runs in behind at the same time, Arsenal’s defenders drop – and Groß has the time for the shot from around 20 metres. In the build-up Brighton had used rotations to drag Guimarães over to the left.

The opening goal stems from a positional attack. Kostoulas spots open space and makes a run into it. With a pass played across his standing leg, he feeds the ball to Groß in the space between the lines. As Groß takes a few quick touches and dribbles toward the defensive line, Gabriel and Calafiori drop back together, thereby opening up a shooting lane.

The 2-0 by Kostoulas shortly before half-time follows the same logic from the opposite direction. After a set piece of their own, Brighton clear an Arsenal counter and transition again immediately, 4v5 in Arsenal’s half, and once more the shot comes from distance while the centre-backs drop off.

Much like the goal that made it 1–0, both defenders went to ground near the ball carrier, thereby opening up space for the goalscorer—this time arising from a transition situation.

According to recent reports, both goals share the same cause: Arsenal’s centre-backs stepped out too late to press the man between the lines. React only when the shooting motion starts and you cannot get into the block from 20 to 25 metres. What is striking is that this passivity is the same one Arsenal highlighted in their own build-up – a side that does not leave its position to offer itself does not leave it to close down a shooter either.

The 3-0 by Chema Andrés came from a corner: Groß delivered from the left, Brighton had created an overload at the far post and protected it with two blocks, and Chema rose completely unmarked to head in off the inside of the post.

According to recent reports, two goals up, many sides would have defended deeper. Brighton came out with unchanged and at times higher pressing intensity, and the coordination was visibly drilled: marking assignments were swapped cleanly even in dynamic situations, and Arsenal’s structural adjustments were absorbed.

Arsenal had managed a few organised possession phases in Brighton’s half in the first period; in the second it became harder. In those phases they built with a back three, Rice as the third centre-back, Ødegaard dropping alongside Guimarães and the full-backs occupying the half-spaces. Arteta reacted around the hour: Zubimendi and Merino for Timber and Guimarães, with Rice moving to right-back, followed shortly by Gyökeres and Eze for Ødegaard and Tzolis. There was no noticeable effect, because the problem did not lie in the shape but in the assignments in front of it.

There was also a layer that usually goes missing in analysis: Brighton used tactical fouls deliberately to stop Arsenal finding a rhythm. Arteta admitted afterwards that the game had been “very difficult to control”, pointing to lost first and second balls and to Brighton’s directness.

In a recent development, arteta’s Arsenal being outplayed this clearly is rare. That it happened proactively and aggressively is rarer still – most sides who take something from Arsenal do it with a low block and efficiency. Hürzeler deliberately stepped back afterwards and praised his players’ courage, which gets to the heart of it: the plan only works if eleven players are willing to carry it through in every single sequence.

In a recent development, the interesting question is where the idea came from. Chelsea were a common opponent: Brighton had 74 per cent possession there and lost 3-4 against a counter-attacking side – control right down to the numbers, without return. Alonso’s Chelsea tried the opposite route against Arsenal, a deliberate surrender of control, also without success. The likely derivation lies between the two: neither give up control nor chase it, but generate the unsettled game state yourself and be prepared for it.

There is no reason for panic at Arsenal, but Arteta will need answers against a high press. The build-up was predictable for long stretches, and above all the direct option with pace in behind was missing as a threat. As long as that does not exist, a man-oriented press costs very little against this side.

According to recent reports, for Brighton the open question is repeatability. Man-marking of this commitment, collective recovery runs with cover shadows and a touchline trap that requires everyone to trigger at once are hard to produce twice in an English week. Whether the plan works was answered on this afternoon. How often it can be produced will decide the season.

Latest Update: Barbra Banda talks a 2021 in which she rose to global prominence and the future

📅 23 Jan 2022 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2032 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thesefootballtimes

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that very few footballers anywhere in the world shot to prominence in 2021 quite like Zambia forward Barbra Banda.
  • It was the very first appearance for the Copper Queens at a women’s football tournament, and ranked outside the world’s top 100, few gave them a chance of competing in a group that included China, Brazil and European champions, the Netherlands.
  • A 10-3 defeat in their opening game against the latter emphasised the gap, but was memorable for the 21-year-old scoring an extraordinary hat-trick, with two or her goals coming in the space of a minute towards the end of the game with the result already beyond doubt.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that very few footballers anywhere in the world shot to prominence in 2021 quite like Zambia forward Barbra Banda. A name familiar to those who follow the women’s game in-depth, but perhaps an unknown to many, Banda changed that in the space of four incredible days during the summer Olympic Games in Tokyo.

It was the very first appearance for the Copper Queens at a women’s football tournament, and ranked outside the world’s top 100, few gave them a chance of competing in a group that included China, Brazil and European champions, the Netherlands.

A 10-3 defeat in their opening game against the latter emphasised the gap, but was memorable for the 21-year-old scoring an extraordinary hat-trick, with two or her goals coming in the space of a minute towards the end of the game with the result already beyond doubt.

As if that wasn’t enough, Banda hit another hat-trick just three days later in a thrilling 4-4 draw against China, becoming the first player ever to score back-to-back Olympic hat-tricks.

Recent findings suggest that sitting in her hotel room in China where she is undergoing mandatory isolation after returning from a national team camp, Banda reflects on a period that propelled into the eyes of the world on the biggest stage available. “I never thought I would represent Zambia on that kind of stage,” she says. “I always told myself it’s about hard work and determination that gets you there and then suddenly I found myself representing my country at an Olympics.”.

Throughout our interview, Banda is humble, but more than anything continuously emphasises how her whole career has, and will continue to be, about hard work, about determination, that she hasn’t yet come close to achieving what she wants, even reflecting that the tournament was somewhat of a disappointment despite what they were up against and the personal history she made.

“We didn’t do our level best to go to the second round, but for our team just being there was a great achievement, for our country, for Africa, because we were the only African team there. It was history for us just to qualify for Tokyo. The achievement of scoring those two hat-tricks, it’s just the result of what kind of person I am. I work hard, I am always there for my team and for my country and all I do is aim to do the best for my country.”.

Despite only turning 21 this year and having a large part of her career still in front of her, it has been a long and eventful journey for Banda just to get to where she is now, growing up in a country where women’s football was far from prominent.

Recent findings suggest that banda joined an academy as a youngster and spent over 10 years there, and it was the motivation she got from her dad in particular which inspired her to continue following her dream. “For me, I started very early, I just used to go and play football with my dad. At the academy, that’s when I started playing competitively in a league for women in Zambia.

“Things happened quite swiftly. At the age of 13 I was called up for trials for the under 17 national team and ended up doing to play in Costa Rica at the under 17 World Cup in Costa Rica.”.

Yes, at the age of just 13, Banda was representing her nation at a major FIFA tournament, where she was incredibly only the second-youngest player behind 12-year-old Ghanaian defender Fuseina Mumuni; a tournament that saw Banda suddenly gracing the same pitches as other promising youngsters such as Deyna Castellanos, Lea Schüller, Jessie Fleming, Patri Guijarro and Aitana Bonmatí.

“After that I moved clubs, went to a bigger club, the Green Buffalos in Zambia. I think that’s when I started with the senior national team and started to become a bit more well-known to people.

Sources indicate that “As time went on I was still so inspired by my dad,” she recalls. “He was always there for me in terms of football. It’s interesting because it was really only him who was interested, my mum didn’t want me to play football. I wanted to play and my dad encouraged me, but my mum wanted me to go to school and get an education. But, now they’re both happy with how I’m doing.”.

By this time Banda was starting to gain attention from around the world as she looked to take the next step in her career, and found an agent, Anton, who is on the call too, with the pair now having worked together for several years and formed a close working relationship.

Several Spanish clubs in particular were interested in signing Banda in the summer of 2018 but weren’t overly convinced about taking who was then a relatively unknown African striker who hadn’t played football outside Zambia.

It has been revealed that there was also the glitch of the looming annual COSAFA Cup in Africa, which would take place in September at the very start of the European season, with several interested clubs demanding Banda miss the tournament. One of those who passed up the opportunity was relegated at the end of the season.

In the end, newly-promoted Logroño took the chance on Banda and the teenager went on to score 16 goals in 28 league appearances for the club across a two-year stay in Spain. “That was a great move or me and I always thank Anton, he has always been there for me,” she smiles. “He knows what it takes to have a player and put trust in that player when nobody else believes in you. He believed in me and made it possible for me to move to Spain.

According to recent reports, “Many clubs wouldn’t accept African players, they didn’t think we were at that level, but I went there and highlighted in Africa that we do have good players. Everyone there was happy with me. The players, the management, everyone was happy. I enjoyed Spain, it was competitive, they love football there and every game was very hard and very strong.”.

Recent findings suggest that it was not just a big move for Banda on the pitch, but off it. It meant a first move away not just from Zambia, but Africa. At the age of 18, Banda was leaving behind everything and everyone she’d ever known in the search of making football a career for her and to show other young girls in Zambia it could be done.

“Being the first time, my parents were a bit worried, but I think there was a good side as well because they’d got used to me going away for weeks and months with the national team. I think that contributed to them understanding, they had to accept it.”.

In a recent development, it wasn’t just her family Banda had to convince either. Extraordinarily, Banda was undergoing mandatory military service in Zambia at the time and had to get permission from the colonel of the Zambian army which she laughs “wasn’t easy” when discussing the story.

In a recent development, “It was so difficult! That’s why I really appreciate Anton, because he worked so hard for me. I was coming from military service, there was a lot of paperwork, a lot of explanations, so it wasn’t easy. The Zambian army commander is now the women’s representative for women’s football in Zambia. She did a lot of good work for me to get permission from the colonel of the army which meant I could go to Spain.”.

At the start of 2020, Banda left Spain and indeed Europe and opted to move to China and play for Shanghai Shengli, but her debut had to wait after the start of the COVID-19 pandemic meant a much more condensed season played over the course of just three months towards the end of the year.

According to recent reports, despite fewer games than planned, Banda scored an incredible 18 goals in her debut season, nine clear of the next best, fellow African forward Temwa Chawinga. “It’s a good league,” she claims. “I came here, did my best and was the top scorer, which was a great achievement for me.”.

Her second year saw her miss a large chunk of the campaign due to her involvement in the Olympic Games, which is still where her most vivid memories remain as she still looks to really take in what she achieved in Tokyo.

Industry observers note that “It has been so overwhelming,” she admits. “I think everyone was proud of me, breaking those records is not easy. A lot of people have passed a lot of compliments about me and I’m happy about that, but I can’t be relaxed about what people comment on and the praise they give me. I have to keep focused on working hard and hopefully breaking more records on top of what I did in the summer.

Industry observers note that “I still maintain the same aims, the same discipline I have always portrayed. I just have to work even harder now to make sure I still have those nice messages from people in the future.”.

It’s a self-image Banda is keen to maintain, wary of the impact she is having not just back home in Zambia, but all around Africa, where she has quickly become one of the most iconic footballers on the continent.

Recent findings suggest that with Zambia now aiming to back up their Olympic Games appearance with a first World Cup in 2023, Banda wants to juggle what she is doing on the pitch with ensuring she remains a role model for young girls off it. “I just have to show a good example to everyone who looks up to me, that’s the most crucial thing. They look up to me and as their icon I have to show good manners so they copy that.

“As soon as I do something bad, I will become a bad example to everyone. The best way to show myself is to stay out of those things. I just have to focus on doing what I’m doing and keep only inspiring more people in my country and around Africa.”.

It’s a role she admits though is “not easy”, especially given the extra reputation she now has off the back of those four incredible days in Tokyo. “I don’t know what to say. I still remember it all the time. I didn’t expect it, I just did my best and I showed what I can do. Like I stated, for me, I still want to work hard and just continue what I’m doing.

According to recent reports, “Women have not always been supported in Zambia, but you saw people cheering us at the Olympics and it has changed since. There is a Champions League now in Africa, I think we are heading somewhere step by step. We don’t feel like we have everything we need as women, but we have shown we are here, we exist, we play the same football. We get positive messages from fans, they are talking about women’s football in Zambia, we are putting it on the map for people.”.

After two years in Spain, it may just be two years in China too, as Banda is looking ahead to the future and what may await her given the attention she has received. While she’s giving little away as to what may lay ahead, it’s clear she has ambitions to make a move to a top team and continue fulfilling her ambitions.

Sources indicate that “I always want to try upcoming things experience football in different clubs and different players. I enjoyed playing here, but if anything comes up I want to experience other kinds of football. I am ok here, I enjoy, it’s a good league, better than people think. I’m still very young. My main target is to play in the Champions League – we will see what happens. I just do what I do, I work hard and hope for the best in my future.”.

Industry observers note that danielle van de Donk opened the scoring in the 14th minute, finishing after an assist from Isobel Goodwin. Palace answered 10 minutes later through Abbie Larkin. Before the interval María Pérez was booked for a foul in the 38th minute.

The hosts took control early in the second half. Alexia Putellas restored the lead in the 51st minute, and van de Donk added her second at 54 minutes. Jamie-Lee Napier was then cautioned for Palace in the 56th minute.

Palace did reply. Annabel Blanchard pulled one back in the 64th minute, set up by Fuka Tsunoda, and finished with five shots and a rating of 7.74, the best of the visiting side.

Any hope of a comeback faded inside four minutes. Alanna Kennedy made it 4-2 in the 73rd minute and Goodwin added a fifth at 77 minutes, both goals created by León. Everett and León were each booked late on before Putellas completed her double in the 89th minute.

In a recent development, putellas was rated 8.75, the highest on the pitch, with Goodwin just behind on 8.74 after a goal, an assist and six shots. León, who played 88 minutes, created five chances and was rated 8.48.

According to recent reports, the scoreline matched the balance of play. London City had 64% of the ball, completed 450 passes to Palace’s 218 and had 25 shots to 9, with 12 on target. Twenty of those attempts came from inside the box. Their expected goals figure was 3 against 0.76 for Palace, so the hosts scored twice as many as their chances suggested.

In a recent development, palace goalkeeper Yáñez made six saves. That still was not enough.

Just the eight goals in Bromley!

It’s a high-scoring victory for London City Lionesses over Crystal Palace, with Daniëlle van de Donk and Alexia Putellas on the scoresheet twice.

The wistful romanticism of ÍA, the club that once ruled Iceland against the odds

📅 23 Jan 2022 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3652 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thesefootballtimes

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A little over 30 miles to the north of Reykjavik resides the small port town of Akranes on Iceland’s west coast.
  • Industry observers note that like many coastal settlements in Iceland, Akranes is noted for its thriving fishing industry, and its deep, still harbour is home to a flotilla of trawlers that combs these teeming waters each summer.
  • Those who do not take to the waves in search of fish prefer to take to the football field in search of a more prestigious catch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A little over 30 miles to the north of Reykjavik resides the small port town of Akranes on Iceland’s west coast. Even for Iceland, this is not a huge place. With its buildings gathered on a thin sliver of a peninsula that extends furtively into the ocean, it is home to a mere 8,000 inhabitants.

Industry observers note that like many coastal settlements in Iceland, Akranes is noted for its thriving fishing industry, and its deep, still harbour is home to a flotilla of trawlers that combs these teeming waters each summer. But there is another reason that Akranes is a name familiar to many Icelanders, and it has nothing to do with trawlermen.

Those who do not take to the waves in search of fish prefer to take to the football field in search of a more prestigious catch. The town’s resident football team, Íþróttabandalag Akraness, more commonly referred to by their initials ÍA, are one of Iceland’s most successful clubs. It is a remarkable feat given that for much of its 75-year existence, the club has been bound by its rural location and small population.

The roots of this success were planted deep in the earth of the 20th century when in 1951 ÍA became the first club outside of Reykjavik to secure the Úrvalsdeild karla title – literally, the Men’s Select Division. For the first 39 years of the league’s existence, the Reykjavik clubs of Knattspyrnufélag Reykjavíkur (KR), Valur, Vikingur and Knattspyrnufélagið Fram had exerted an unshakeable oligopoly over Iceland’s elite football division.

But throughout the latter half of the century, as the league moved beyond a single-round to a double-round format, the inhabitants of this small fishing town became famed for their excellence on the football pitch. Between 1951 and 1990, no club was as successful in Iceland as ÍA, and much of this domestic dominance was attributed to the labours of Ríkharður Jonsson, who acted as long-time player-manager.

Sadly, he passed away in 2017, but These Football Times was privileged enough to speak with his daughter, Sigrún Ríkharðsdóttir, with help from his grandson, Ríkharður Árnason. Sigrún has been attending ÍA matches her entire life and is as fervent a Skagamenn supporter as they come. “You don’t want to sit next to me at a game,” she notes drily. “I am the loudest woman in Iceland when it comes to the football!” Meanwhile, her son shares his first name with the legendary figure of his grandfather and is head of social media at the club. Few, if any, can claim a richer heritage with this unique football club.

Their past and their future are incorrigibly entwined with that of Íþróttabandalag Akraness, and it is in their past that this tale begins. In 1990, to be precise, whereupon ÍA had suffered relegation for only the second time in their history. Though they had won the league twice and the Icelandic Cup four times throughout the 1980s, by the turn of the decade the club had somehow contrived to slip through the dreaded trapdoor into the First League.

“You know how football is,” Sigrún Ríkharðsdóttir notes with a wry smile when asked to explain what went wrong for the then-12-time champions. “Sometimes you have a good game. Sometimes you have a bad game. But the team from ’83 and ’84 were gone, and the next generation we had taking over were young – very young, indeed.”.

Industry observers note that the ÍA team that suffered the infamy of relegation was heavily reliant on a core of young and painfully inexperienced footballers. Several of the players who featured in every, or almost every, league game included left winger Haraldur Ingólfsson (20-years-old), midfielder/left-back Sigursteinn Gíslason (22) and future superstar striker Arnar Gunnlaugsson, who was the team’s joint top-scorer that season at the mere age of 17.

Industry observers note that admirable though it was to entrust the fortunes of the club in the hands (and feet) of youth, the result for ÍA was painful. Playing football in the second tier for the first time since 1968, this predicament only consolidated the view in Reykjavik that Akranes was simply a town of chancers who had punched far above their weight for far too long and were now reaping what they’d sown in their foolhardy attempts to meddle with the might of the capital.

Industry observers note that realising that the club had been allowed to slowly decay throughout the latter half of the 1980s, the board turned to one of its former stalwarts to invigorate an inexperienced squad in need of firm guidance. ÍA legend and all-time appearance holder, Guðjón Þórðarson, was persuaded to rejoin the club at which he had found fame in his playing days.

One of the last relics of the 1980s golden era, since retiring in 1987 he had ventured into coaching and his innovative training methods, which placed an enormous emphasis on fitness, discipline and recovery, had seen virtual unknowns KA Akureyri crowned champions for the first time in their history by virtue of being fitter, faster and better organised than their contemporaries.

In a recent development, he was a man in high demand, but with KA lacking the finances required to repeat this success in subsequent seasons, the chance of a reunion with ÍA proved too alluring to ignore. Even though it necessitated dropping down a division, he agreed to become head coach and began in earnest restoring ÍA to the Úrvalsdeild karla.

The only previous time ÍA had suffered relegation had resulted in an immediate return to the top flight, whereupon they finished second, before going one better and winning the league the following year in 1970. Accordingly, great things were expected of this dynamic side brimming with youthful vigour, and under the strict stewardship of Þórðarson, they were being moulded into a formidable outfit.

Serendipity deigned to alight upon ÍA who, despite playing football in the unglamorous environment of Iceland’s second division, managed to attract the services of three players patently too talented for their surroundings. First, Þórðarson – who was renowned for travelling extensively on his scholastic enterprises – spotted the hulking figure of Olafur Adolfsson in the amateur leagues of Iceland’s sparse northern marches and brought him to Akranes. At well over six feet tall and broad of shoulder and limb too, Adolfsson struck an uncompromising figure at the heart of the ÍA back line.

Industry observers note that alongside this mountain of a man, Þórðarson installed Luka Kostic, a Yugoslav centre-half who is, even to this day, widely regarded as the finest foreign footballer to have ever played in Iceland, even though he was 33 at the time of his arrival. Bringing with him a wealth of expertise, he was responsible for marshalling those around him.

Boasting an impregnable defence aided by the capture from bitter rivals KR of 20-year-old goalkeeper Kristján Finnbogason, ÍA made predictably short work of returning to the top flight. Across 18 second division games in 1991, the club won 14, scored 55 goals and conceded a paltry 12 in reply. Úrvalsdeild karla football ensured for the 1992 campaign, hope slunk back into Akranes. With the most innovative young manager in the country presiding over a hungry, well-drilled squad of saplings primed to flourish come spring, there was a feeling ÍA could cause an upset.

However, since Skagamenn’s last championship victory in 1984, Fram and Valur had asserted their domestic dominance. The two traditionally powerful Reykjavik clubs had won five of the previous seven titles, and on three occasions occupied first and second places in the league. Even with ÍA’s return, the title was widely expected to remain in the capital, at least for another year. From the outside, the yellow-clad upstarts from Akranes were still too inexperienced to mount a serious title challenge so soon after the turmoil of relegation and were written off by pundits, supporters and near enough anyone with even a passing interest in Icelandic football.

However, before the season began in 1992, ÍA were to benefit from one more fortuitous occurrence, one which would have a major bearing on their fortunes for years to come, as Þórðarson convinced former player Sigurður Jónsson to make the long trip back to his hometown.

Only 25-years-old at the time, the prodigious midfielder had been forced to retire prematurely after suffering a back injury while playing for Arsenal in England’s old First Division but was coaxed into playing once more for the club at which he made his debut aged just 15. A veritable legend of the sport in Iceland, he was the erstwhile youngest debutant in a European game before being supplanted by a certain Martin Ødegaard some years later.

Much to the chagrin of the Reykjavik clubs – and in particular their fierce rivals KR – ÍA furnished their return to the Úrvalsdeild karla with their 13th championship and their first in nearly a decade.

It was a momentous achievement, which Ríkharðsdóttir ascribes in part, at least, to patience. “Many of the boys who were with us when we fell down to the First League stayed with us and these young lads just got stronger and better [under Þórðarson].”.

Inclined to set-up in a four-four-two system that harnessed a squad accustomed to gruelling training regimens, the ÍA players ran harder and for longer, were physically stronger and, as is crucial to any team with ambitions of winning a league, possessed an indomitable mental resilience in pursuit of their goals. That they could play, too, was an added benefit.

According to recent reports, although it is not unheard of for clubs to win the title immediately after promotion, especially in the Nordic countries where the traditionally smaller leagues are somewhat renowned for producing surprise victors, seldom have many teams managed to repeat the feat. Indeed, miraculously, ÍA became the first club in the history of football to not only win the league following promotion but win it for five consecutive seasons.

It has been revealed that just how could a team hailing from a town of barely 8,000 people, and who had been relegated just a year earlier, undertake a championship run the likes of which had never been witnessed in Iceland in over a century of organised sport? Not just Iceland, either, but anywhere in the entire world. At the time, no team had won five championships in a row directly after being promoted. It was an idea born from fiction; a feat literally unbelievable in its design.

Industry observers note that ríkharðsdóttir, however, believes she has the answer. “It was the same team. All the five years. And the manager, too. In 1992, 1993, and 1996 we had the same manager [Guðjón Þórðarson].”.

Sources indicate that this continuity undoubtedly benefited ÍA, but there was another factor at play, one which, in the long roster of champions not just in Iceland but across the continent of Europe, is unquestionably unique. Though many claim to be ‘close-knit family clubs’ nowhere is it more pertinent than in Akranes, where, it is stated, “everyone is related somewhere”.

Of ÍA’s squad, eight were sons of former players, seven were brothers, six were cousins, three were nephews and, in a testament to the longevity of this dynasty, one was even a grandson. Ríkharðsdóttir herself, being the daughter of the club’s most famous player, claims a deep affinity within this 1990s vintage side. “In that team at the beginning of the 1990s, I had four uncles. In fact, lots of good local players are in the same families here,” she explains.

It is an entirely unique footballing dynasty; a positive myriad of interrelated riches. But clearly, as the old adage goes, there is something in the water in Akranes, for such a small town to repeatedly produce an unbroken line of talent that coaching alone cannot surely engender. Genetics play their part, and Ríkharðsdóttir explains with an air of pride the stats behind her town’s unmatched footballing pedigree. “We have had 38 players [as of 2021] that have played professionally abroad. That is 0.5 percent of the town’s current population who are or were professional footballers playing around the world.”.

Given the small size of town, it is scarcely believable that this tiny strip of land on Iceland’s west coast has been so prolific in producing such talented footballers. Fortunately for ÍA in the 1990s, they profited from the particularly abundant vintage of 1973, which produced the likes of Arnar Gunnlaugsson, Þórður Guðjónsson and Lárus Orri Sigurðsson, all of whom were raised and nurtured in Akranes. Though they went on to enjoy careers in England’s Premier League, it was their exploits between 1992 and 1996 that earned them acclaim in their town of provenance.

Over the course of five years, ÍA stormed to five consecutive league titles. After the first was secured on their return to the Úrvalsdeild karla by a three-point margin, a rivalry that had been put on pause during their relegation reignited. Enmity had been simmering between ÍA and KR in the years prior to 1992, and with the latter enduring a protracted silverware drought, the notion of ÍA returning to the pinnacle of Icelandic football rekindled this latent wrath.

Recent findings suggest that the 1993 season, therefore, was billed as a clash between two eternal enemies, but, once again, pundits and observers alike dismissed ÍA’s chances of repeating their 1992 success. At the time in the early-90s, KR were the only club capable of paying their players anything close to what would now be regarded as a professional salary, and as such could attract the finest players to West Reykjavik. Their riches could not stop ÍA romping to a second title in two years, however.

Sources indicate that if anything, ÍA were, to the surprise of many, merely waxing in strength. In 1992, they had amassed 40 points from 12 wins and four draws, but in 1993 they finished top of the pile with an incredulous 49 points – a full nine points clear of nearest challengers FH. Indeed, only Fram took any points whatsoever off Skagamenn that year. The rest of the league stumbled in their efforts to keep up with the early pace set by Þórðarson’s insatiable side. On no fewer than seven occasions, ÍA scored four or more goals in a single game, including an opening day 5-0 demolition of eventual runners-up FH.

Þórður Guðjónsson, of the famed 1973 vintage, finished as both club and league top scorer with 19 goals, while 22-year-old winger Haraldur Ingólfsson was not far behind with 14. Moreover, that ÍA could outscore virtually anyone was daunting enough, but their resolute backline was breached only 12 times all season – and seven of those came during the two fixtures with Fram.

It has been revealed that it was inevitable, then, that ÍA would march to a third title in a row in 1994, but not without KR attempting everything in their power to ensure otherwise. After they had finished in a lowly fifth in 1993, having been unceremoniously thumped by ÍA to the tune of five goals over two fixtures, the Reykjavik giants sought to undercut their rivals the only way they knew how: money. They lured manager Guðjón Þórðarson to the KR-völlur and secured the return of goalkeeper Kristján Finnbogason. Little did it matter, though, for Þórðarson had bred a monster even he himself could not slay, no matter the riches with which he tempered his sword.

According to recent reports, KR finished fifth again, while ÍA clinched a hat-trick of championships. Not that the season was without its struggles. In the absence of Þórðarson, the board had appointed Hörður Helgason, and though he won the title, he was more alike to a custodian than manager. Compared to 1992, when Skagamenn had marched to 16 wins, they faltered to three 0-0 draws and three losses in a season which saw their goal tally plummet from 55 to 35. Mistrusted by the players, who allegedly did not approve of his outdated coaching methods, he was dismissed at the end of the year and replaced with Logi Ólafsson.

Þórðarson, meanwhile, attempted to navigate KR back to the summit of the Úrvalsdeild karla in 1994 and perhaps would have done so had Olafsson not reinvigorated ÍA with his arrival. Yet again, the club came perilously close to that elusive unbeaten campaign, as they registered just a single loss – ironically, to Þórðarson’s KR side, who would eventually finish a very distant second to their bitter rivals. For the fourth season in a row, an ÍA player finished as the league’s top scorer; this time, it was another member of the 1973 vintage, Arnar Gunnlaugsson, who completed the campaign with 15 goals to his name.

According to recent reports, in 1996, Þórðarson, whose affair with KR had come to an unsavoury end, returned to the club, looking to secure a fifth consecutive title and his third with ÍA. Astonishingly, KR were installed as the strong favourites for the title, and for once, the bookies were almost right.

Recent findings suggest that for the first time in five years, Iceland witnessed an enthralling title race between two heated enemies, where over the course of 17 games, the two clubs exchanged places at the top of the table before a final-day show down at the Akranesvöllur. KR had emerged victorious in the return fixture, a 1-0 win courtesy of a 68th-minute Ríkharður Daðason goal, but the final day clash is a day Sigrún Ríkharðsdóttir recalls fondly, and for more than one reason. “In 1996, in the last game we played against KR, and KR needed just a draw to win the title. But we had to win. And, oh my god, we did. Four goals against one.”.

ÍA, who had been trailing KR for much of the campaign, demonstrated the enormous mental resolve for which they had become renowned, and overhauled the leaders on the final day of the season. Knowing that a draw was all KR required, they tore into their opponents, going 2-0 up by the hour-mark before Ríkharður Daðason pulled one back to set up a nervy final twenty minutes. It is a name familiar to many in Akranes, especially Sigrún Ríkharðsdóttir.

“The scorer for the KR goal was [her son] Rikki’s uncle and namesake! For that one goal he scored that game, he won the golden boot.”.

According to recent reports, unfortunately for Sigrún Ríkharðsdóttir, Ríkharður Árnason and the inhabitants of Akranes, the 1996 league and cup double marked the end of a record-breaking cycle. By 1997, the yellow-and-black stranglehold on the Úrvalsdeild karla had slackened, but the relinquishing of their throne was at least a slow and reluctant process, for ÍA still managed to finish second in 1997, then third in 1998 and even reigned as champions again, albeit briefly, in 2001.

What precipitated the downfall of their monopoly was a convergence of many factors, Ríkharðsdóttir believes. “Our key players have gone away, both to play abroad and for other teams in Iceland. For me, it’s extremely difficult to watch my boys play for other teams in Iceland.”.

This assertion harks back to the notion that football in Akranes remains very much a familial affair. Those who come through the ranks at ÍA are Skagamenn until the end of their days, even if their travels are increasingly taking them farther and farther from home.

Recent findings suggest that “It is also a question of money,” Ríkharðsdóttir continues. “The main thing today is that because we are not in European competition, we do not have enough money. Our players prefer to go abroad. One of our players is in CSKA Moscow [Arnór Sigurðsson] and one of our boys plays for Norrköping [Oliver Stefánsson].”.

Similarly, prodigious winger Ísak Bergmann Jóhannesson, who has drawn the attention of a host of clubs across the continent, plies his trade with FC København, while Stefán Teitur Þórðarson went to Silkeborg in Denmark and Bjarki Steinn Bjarkason is enjoying Serie A football with Venezia.

Recent findings suggest that unfortunately for ÍA, when the club was in its pomp in the early to mid-90s, European qualification was nowhere near as lucrative as it is today. They made fleeting appearances in the UEFA Champions League preliminary round in 1993 and the UEFA Cup first round between 1994 and 1997, but without the enormous financial rewards gleaned by the continental voyages of today’s top teams in Iceland.

In a recent development, as such, it has been a long 20 years since the club’s last title in 2001. An Icelandic Cup victory in 2003 and a runners-up medal in 2021 have provided scant solace for the proud people of Akranes who grow ever more restless with each barren season. This two-decade stretch marks the longest period in their history they have gone without winning the league, and in that time they have been relegated twice, albeit returning to the top flight at the first time of asking on both occasions.

There have been no more five-in-a-row heroics, though, as an increasingly globalised world, which has seen Icelandic football broadcast to the rest of Europe for the first time in the league’s history, has led on one hand to a diaspora of Akranes’ young footballers and on the other to an influx of foreign talent to the traditionally powerful Reykjavik clubs.

Silverware will return, the people of Akranes believe; after all, their town is the fastest growing settlement in all of Iceland, and therein lies a sliver of hope. Amidst the squabbling rich boys of Reykjavik, there still may be a place for the wistful romanticism of ÍA. Perhaps, in years to come, another legacy in yellow-and-black will emerge from this westerly stronghold of dynastic riches – born of fresh blood within which is carried the blueprint of that unrivalled 1990s vintage.

With thanks to Sígrun Ríkharðsdóttir, Ríkharður Árnason, Bjarki Ármannsson and Mike Morgan.

Talking to Icarus Football, the kit designers adding beauty to the game

📅 24 Jan 2022 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1094 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thesefootballtimes

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Football shirts give off a lot of signals,” Robby Smukler indicates.
  • Industry observers note that it’s easy to agree with that sentiment.
  • You might also say that they’re a great way of telling your nosey Red neighbour that you’re a die-hard Blue in that silent “fuck you” kind of way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Football shirts give off a lot of signals,” Robby Smukler indicates. “They can indicate what you’re passionate about, where you’re from, and even your politics in some cases. That’s part of what makes them so special as a piece of clothing—there’s really so much that’s tied into a football shirt.”.

Industry observers note that it’s easy to agree with that sentiment. Combining place, philosophy, art, design, and, for some, religion and a sense of belonging, football shirts are the acceptable fashion piece that allow anyone to make a splash and stand out from the crowd. Whether worn at a match, at a festival, or for a quick trip to the coffee house, jerseys are the accessible statement piece anyone can pull off (or on) with ease.

You might also say that they’re a great way of telling your nosey Red neighbour that you’re a die-hard Blue in that silent “fuck you” kind of way.

Robby is the founder of Icarus Football, a custom kit design service making tailor-made shirts for everyone, from five-a-side teams to semi-pro outfits. Quintessentially one-of-a-kind, their jerseys offer one-off pieces that faithfully highlight the sui generis of each club.

Robby’s dream of being a creative started many years ago when he became fascinated with sketching football-themed creations at an early age. As a child growing up in Philadelphia, he would read up on cities and countries near and far before making jersey and crest designs to pass the time.

From the get-go, imagination and flair were key parts of his approach, and that has continued to this day, allowing him to realize all sorts of concepts for teams from a myriad of backgrounds. “We design shirts with fans of a club in mind rather than players. And fans are increasingly looking for creative designs to wear, whether that be for pick-up games in the park or music festivals.

According to recent reports, “I think part of the appeal comes from the colours and designs used on football kits. They’re often a lot more creative and out-there than traditional men’s clothing, so football shirts offer something different. They’re also comfortable, so they fit in with the growing trend towards athleisure,” Robby explains.

Indeed, football jerseys are very in today; whether it’s the fresh releases by the top clubs or the retro classic continually making a comeback, there is a lot of demand for eye-catching sportswear.

It has been revealed that icarus Football’s jerseys appeal to a wide audience because they are steeped in personality, unique designs, and more. As Robby explains, the shirts they make are inspired by each club’s “history, iconography, imagery, fan culture, location”, offering an antidote to the bland factory-manufactured shirts that clubs and fans are often forced to buy.

Robby and his team offer distinctive, eye-catching shirts that clubs can wear with pride when they take to the field. Fans, too, can appreciate the carnival of colour that defines many of their creations, the tailored detail of the pieces, and the thoughtful artistry, too.

Sources indicate that “For us, a design that references a team’s culture and history makes a shirt special. But for it to be totally iconic–it needs to be worn in an interesting context.

“The Holland ’88 and Germany ’90 jerseys are two of the most iconic designs of all time, and deservedly so. They’re amazing designs. But if they weren’t worn by those trophy-winning teams and wrapped up in those historic moments, I don’t think they would be considered as legendary as they are.

Recent findings suggest that “The moments in which shirts are worn and the players that wear them both contribute to the status of a shirt. That also speaks a little bit as to why retro shirts have become so popular.

According to recent reports, “Legendary players from the 80s/90s seem cooler, perhaps because a lot of young people didn’t get to watch them play during their careers. Only getting to watch legends like [Gheorge] Hagi, [Marco] Van Basten, [Johan] Cruyff, [Michael] Laudrup, [Roberto] Baggio …through limited YouTube videos and highlight reels makes them appear all the more legendary. And that rubs off a bit on the status of the shirts that they wore.”.

Robbie’s thoughts confirm the notion that retro jerseys have long been on the comeback trail.

Instagram is full of posts with throwbacks to iconic shirts of old – and to football’s traditions and magical teams. Boca Juniors, Fiorentina, Liverpool, AC Milan, Paris Saint-Germain, Barcelona, and more are just some of the clubs that feature heavily in posts dripping with charm, style, and those-were-the-days vibes.

After all, what football fan can scroll past a post of Diego Maradona in the pomp of his career wearing that special Mars-sponsored Napoli shirt without leaving an emphatic ‘like’?

Recent findings suggest that nostalgia is a major art of the apparent resurgence in popularity of retro replicas, but kit designer Robbie also believes retro shirts are popular because of something else, too “Retro shirts are baggier and made from materials that are almost closer to modern-day sweatshirts than football shirts. That plays well when it comes to fashion.”.

Indeed, Icarus Football’s line of historical concept jerseys speaks to how sought-after retro-style kits are. “We really love working on our historical jersey range. We love history, and these jerseys are playful attempts at football shirts for bygone civilizations (e.g., Ancient Egypt, Mesopotamia, The Republic of Venice, The Mongol Empire). There’s so much content to use as inspiration for these designs.”.

In a recent development, new Amsterdam FC and Louisiana Krewe are two clubs Icarus FC have worked with in recent times, and they have also worked with clubs in the Ghana Premier League, among so many others. For several years, they have provided a nonconformist approach to fashioning beautiful jerseys shining with distinction. So, what about the future – what teams would Robby and his crew like to work with?

“At a top, top level, it would have to be a national team that’s open to something creative and experimental. National sides have so much imagery, history, and iconography that can be used for the purposes of a personal design. As a geography nerd, I’m extremely interested in working with national sides off the beaten path.

In a recent development, “I’d get just as much joy out of creating a design for Belize as for Brazil. Same thing goes for clubs. Give me TP Mazembe in the Congo, FC Noah in Armenia, and FC Ulaanbaatar in Mongolia (just to name a few) and I’d be a happy man.”.
